steps.explain: One entry per memory cell (byte address) touched this tick, so a cell read twice still lights once.
Each access covers `length` bytes from `address`: walk every one of them, stopping at the end of memory.
A write wins: if this cell was already written this tick, a read of it doesn't change how it lights.
Remember what happened to the cell, and which core (and which part) did it, for its colour and its tooltip.
The map from address to what happened: what `MemoryLayer` lights.
Questions (`mem.read`, `mem.write`) go out first; answers (`mem.data`, `mem.ack`) come back in the second half of the tick, after memory has had them.
Each packet travels for 40% of the tick, starting at its own moment: questions at 5%, answers at 50%.
The other packets don't change this rule; they're there for a board that wants to stagger them.
Outside its moment the packet isn't on the wire (null). Inside, how far along it is, from 0 at the start to 1 at the end.
What each cell did this tick, from `cellActivity`.
Draw a title over the memory area, then the grid: one small square per byte, in rows of `MEMORY_COLUMNS`.
A cell's colour: read or written this tick, the colour of the core that did it (yellow when no core did, like a program load); else a soft green if it holds something, or nothing.
Hovering a cell says its address, its value, and what happened to it this tick.
Where each part sits on the board, and the short word each kind of packet shows.
The parts to draw here: everything but the CPU and memory, which have their own areas.
Draw the bus, a wire from each part up to it, and each peripheral as a box with its name under it and its state inside ("You", the keyboard, is white).
Then each packet of this tick, on the wire from its sender to its receiver, if it's travelling right now (`packetProgress`).
A core's packets take its colour; interrupts are red; everything else is grey.
The tick is over only when every clocked part has said `tick.done` AND every request sent this tick has had its reply. Otherwise a reply could land in the next tick.
`request()` gives back a Promise: the caller awaits it until the matching reply arrives.
Send the message; `send` gives it a fresh id (the ticket number).
Park this request's resolve and reject under that id. When a reply with `replyTo` = id arrives, the client's message handler finds them here and settles the Promise.
The bus says a new tick has started: remember its number (every message this part sends is stamped with it).
Let this part do its work for the tick (each handler registered with `onTick`).
Tell the bus this part is done with the tick, so the bus can count it in the tick barrier.
The handshake is a Promise: it resolves with the bus's `welcome`, or rejects with a clear error.
Every message from the bus arrives as text: parse it, and ignore anything that isn't a valid message.
`welcome` means we're in: stop listening here (the client's own handler takes over) and resolve.
`error` means the bus refused us (say, the id is taken): close the socket and reject, with the bus's reason.
Listen for replies, and fail clearly if the socket can't reach the bus at all.
Once the socket is open, say `hello`: who we are (id, role, label) as an envelope to the bus, at tick 0.
A read: look up the bytes in memory.
Outside memory: answer with a `fault`, so the asker always hears back.
Otherwise remember the read (the board shows it) and reply `mem.data` with the bytes.
A write (or a program being loaded): write the bytes into memory.
Outside memory: a `fault` again.
Otherwise keep the new memory, remember the write, and reply `mem.ack` so the writer knows it happened.
Every byte asked for must be inside memory; if one isn't, say why with a fault.
Otherwise return a copy of those `length` bytes (a slice, so the caller can't change memory through it).
Every byte written must land inside memory.
And every value must fit in a byte: a whole number from 0 to 255.
Memory is never changed in place: copy it, put the bytes in the copy, and return the copy.
First, is it JSON at all? If not, say so instead of crashing.
Then check it against `messageSchema`: the right fields with the right types, for its message type. If not, return the schema's explanation.
Only now is it a `Message` the rest of NetSim can trust.
